records.source: Καὶ ἀναστὰν ἅπαν τὸ πλῆθος αὐτῶν ἤγαγον αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὸν Πιλᾶτον.
records.gloss: And having risen up all the multitude of them led him to the Pilate.
pieces: Then the whole assembly got up and brought {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} before Pilate.

L.1: And the whole multitude of them rose up and led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to Pilate.

R.1: Then the whole council got up and took Jesus to Pilate.

decisions.choice: the whole multitude of them: the council that had questioned Jesus
decisions.reason: "Them" points back to the elders, chief priests and scribes who met as the council at daybreak (22:66). The people and the crowds join later (23:4, 13).

decisions.choice: Pilate: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Pilate governed Judea for the emperor (3:1), from about AD 26 to 36. The council could not carry out a death sentence on its own authority (John 18:31), so it brought Jesus to him.

decisions.choice: the whole council
decisions.reason: Readable says who the multitude was, as the context shows.

records.heading: Jesus is brought to Pilate

records.source: ἤρξαντο δὲ κατηγορεῖν αὐτοῦ λέγοντες· Τοῦτον εὕραμεν διαστρέφοντα τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν καὶ κωλύοντα φόρους Καίσαρι διδόναι καὶ λέγοντα αὑτὸν χριστὸν βασιλέα εἶναι.
records.gloss: They began then to accuse him saying, This [man] we found misleading the nation of us and forbidding tributes to Caesar to give and saying himself Christ a king to be.
pieces: They started to bring charges against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "We have found this man leading our nation astray. He forbids paying taxes to Caesar, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} claims to be {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, a king."

L.2: And they began to accuse {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding [us] to pay taxes to Caesar and saying that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} is {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, a king."

R.2: They began to accuse Jesus. They said, "We caught this man leading our people the wrong way. He tells them not to pay taxes to Caesar. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, a king!"

decisions.choice: misleading: turning people aside, leading them astray
alternatives: teaching wrongly about the law only
decisions.reason: The verb means to twist or turn aside. Before a Roman governor it suggests stirring up the nation against Rome; the charge comes back in other words in 23:5 and 23:14.

decisions.choice: forbidding taxes to Caesar: a false charge
alternatives: a true report of Jesus' teaching
decisions.reason: When he was asked about the tax, Jesus had said to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar (20:22-25). Luke lets the reader see that the charge twists his words.

decisions.choice: Christ, a king: the Jewish title explained as a political claim
alternatives: Christ as a religious title only
decisions.reason: The accusers add "a king" to the title Christ, the anointed King of Israel (9:20), so that Pilate hears a claim to rule in Caesar's place. To Rome that was rebellion.

decisions.choice: himself: he claims it for himself
decisions.reason: The pronoun is reflexive: the charge is that Jesus makes the claim about himself.

decisions.choice: taxes
decisions.reason: The word is for the tax a subject people paid to Rome. "Tribute" is less familiar.

decisions.choice: Christ as the default, Messiah as the alternative
decisions.reason: The title follows the christos setting, as everywhere else.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος ἠρώτησεν αὐτὸν λέγων· Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων;
records.gloss: The but Pilate questioned him saying, You are the king of the Jews?
pieces: So Pilate asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the king of the Jews?"

L.3: And Pilate questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the king of the Jews?"

R.3: Pilate asked Jesus, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the king of the Jews?"

decisions.choice: you: emphatic, set first in the question
decisions.reason: The pronoun stands first and is not needed for the sense. Pilate may be surprised that the man before him is said to be a king.

decisions.choice: the king of the Jews: the title as a Gentile would put it
decisions.reason: Jews spoke of "the king of Israel" (Mark 15:32); "king of the Jews" is how outsiders put it (Matthew 2:2). For Rome, anyone who called himself king without Caesar's leave was a rebel.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς αὐτῷ ἔφη· Σὺ λέγεις.
records.gloss: The and answering him he said, You say.
pieces: He answered him, "You say so."

L.3: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} answered him and said, "You say [so]."

R.3: Jesus answered, "You are the one who says it."

decisions.choice: You say so: a reply that does not deny the title but leaves the words with Pilate
alternatives: a denial: that is your word, not mine
decisions.reason: Jesus gave the council a similar answer (22:70), and they took it as a yes (22:71). Here he does not reject the title, but he does not take it up in Pilate's sense either; Pilate goes on to find no guilt in him (23:4), so he did not hear it as a confession of rebellion.

decisions.choice: You are the one who says it
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the reserve of the answer rather than turning it into a plain yes or no.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Πιλᾶτος εἶπεν πρὸς τοὺς ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ τοὺς ὄχλους· Οὐδὲν εὑρίσκω αἴτιον ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τούτῳ.
records.gloss: The but Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, Nothing I find guilt in the man this.
pieces: Pilate told the chief priests and the crowds, "I find this man guilty of nothing."

L.4: And Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, "I find no guilt in this man."

R.4: Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, "I do not see that this man has done anything wrong."

decisions.choice: guilt: ground for a charge in law
decisions.reason: The word is a legal one: the cause or ground for which a person can be charged and punished. Pilate finds nothing to convict Jesus of.

decisions.choice: the first of three times Pilate declares Jesus innocent
decisions.reason: Pilate says it again in 23:14-15 and a third time in 23:22. Luke shows that the Roman judge did not find Jesus guilty of the charges (Acts 13:28).

decisions.choice: the crowds: people now gathered at Pilate's court
decisions.reason: Crowds appear for the first time in the trial. Until now the people had listened to Jesus gladly (19:48; 21:38).

decisions.choice: I find this man guilty of nothing (B); I do not see that he has done anything wrong (R)
alternatives: I find no guilt in this man
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the verdict in plain words.

records.source: οἱ δὲ ἐπίσχυον λέγοντες ὅτι Ἀνασείει τὸν λαὸν διδάσκων καθ’ ὅλης τῆς Ἰουδαίας, καὶ ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τῆς Γαλιλαίας ἕως ὧδε.
records.gloss: They but kept insisting saying that He stirs up the people teaching throughout all the Judea, and having begun from the Galilee even to here.
pieces: But they pressed the charge harder: "He is stirring up the people with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} teaching all over Judea. He started in Galilee and has come all the way here."

L.5: But they kept insisting, saying, "He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, and having begun from Galilee even to here."

R.5: But they kept on saying, "He is getting the people all stirred up by what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} teaches. He has done it everywhere in Judea. He started in Galilee, and now {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has come here!"

decisions.choice: stirs up: incites, shakes the people into unrest
decisions.reason: The verb pictures shaking something violently; it is used for stirring a crowd to riot. The charge is no longer only about words but about disorder.

decisions.choice: Judea: the whole land of the Jews
alternatives: the Roman province of Judea only
decisions.reason: Luke sometimes uses Judea for the whole country, Galilee included (4:44; 7:17). Peter sums up Jesus' ministry in the same way, "throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee" (Acts 10:37).

decisions.choice: having begun from Galilee: the word Galilee leads into the next scene
decisions.reason: The mention of Galilee prompts Pilate's question in 23:6.

decisions.choice: pressed the charge harder
decisions.reason: The verb means to grow stronger or to insist more. Balanced says what they were insisting on.

records.source: Πιλᾶτος δὲ ἀκούσας ἐπηρώτησεν εἰ ὁ ἄνθρωπος Γαλιλαῖός ἐστιν, καὶ ἐπιγνοὺς ὅτι ἐκ τῆς ἐξουσίας Ἡρῴδου ἐστὶν ἀνέπεμψεν αὐτὸν πρὸς Ἡρῴδην, ὄντα καὶ αὐτὸν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐν ταύταις ταῖς ἡμέραις.
records.gloss: Pilate now having heard asked whether the man a Galilean is, \v 7 and having learned that from the jurisdiction of Herod he is he sent up him to Herod, being also himself in Jerusalem in these the days.
pieces: When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was from Galilee.
When he learned that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came under Herod's authority, he sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} on to Herod, who was also in Jerusalem at that time.

L.6: And when Pilate heard [this], he asked whether the man was a Galilean,
L.7: and having learned that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was from Herod's jurisdiction, he sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} up to Herod, who was himself also in Jerusalem in those days.

R.6: When Pilate heard this, he asked if Jesus came from Galilee.
R.7: He found out that Jesus was from the area that Herod ruled. So he sent Jesus to Herod. Herod was in Jerusalem at that time too.

decisions.choice: Herod: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee
decisions.reason: This is the son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea for Rome (3:1). He had John the Baptist beheaded (9:9), and Pharisees once warned that he wanted to kill Jesus (13:31).

decisions.choice: jurisdiction: the area under his authority
decisions.reason: The word for authority here means the territory over which a ruler has the right to judge.

decisions.choice: sent up: referred the case to another authority
decisions.reason: The verb was used for sending a case on to another court. It is used again when Herod sends Jesus back (23:11, 15).

decisions.choice: Herod was in Jerusalem: for the Passover
decisions.reason: Herod's capital was in Galilee; he had come to Jerusalem for the feast (22:1).

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, since Pilate, Herod and Jesus all appear in the sentence.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Ἡρῴδης ἰδὼν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐχάρη λίαν, ἦν γὰρ ἐξ ἱκανῶν χρόνων θέλων ἰδεῖν αὐτὸν διὰ τὸ ἀκούειν περὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἤλπιζέν τι σημεῖον ἰδεῖν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γινόμενον.
records.gloss: The and Herod having seen the Jesus was glad exceedingly, he was for of long times wishing to see him because of the hearing about him, and he was hoping some sign to see by him done.
pieces: Herod was delighted when he saw Jesus. He had wanted to see {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for a long time because of what he had heard about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and he hoped to watch {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} perform some sign.

L.8: And when Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had been wanting to see {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for a long time because he had been hearing about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and he was hoping to see some sign done by {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.8: Herod was very happy to see Jesus. He had heard about Jesus and had wanted to meet {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for a long time. He hoped Jesus would do some sign, a miracle, while he watched.

decisions.choice: he had long wanted to see him: as Luke said in 9:9
decisions.reason: When Herod heard of Jesus' works, he asked who this was and tried to see him (9:7-9).

decisions.choice: sign: a miracle that would prove who Jesus was
decisions.reason: Herod wants a display. Jesus had refused to give signs to those who demanded them (11:16, 29).

decisions.choice: he was hoping: a continuing hope
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense describes a hope he had held for some time.

decisions.choice: some sign, a miracle
decisions.reason: Readable explains what kind of sign Herod wanted.

records.source: ἐπηρώτα δὲ αὐτὸν ἐν λόγοις ἱκανοῖς· αὐτὸς δὲ οὐδὲν ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: He kept questioning then him in words many; he but nothing answered him.
pieces: He put question after question to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, but Jesus gave him no answer at all.

L.9: And he questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} at length, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} answered him nothing.

R.9: Herod asked Jesus many questions. But Jesus did not answer him at all.

decisions.choice: he answered him nothing: the silent servant
decisions.reason: Isaiah 53:7 speaks of the servant who did not open his mouth, like a sheep before its shearers; Acts 8:32-35 applies that passage to Jesus.

decisions.choice: he: emphatic, in contrast to Herod
decisions.reason: The pronoun is set against Herod's many words: Herod talks, but Jesus says nothing.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus, since both men are "he".

records.source: εἱστήκεισαν δὲ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς εὐτόνως κατηγοροῦντες αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Had been standing now the chief priests and the scribes vehemently accusing him.
pieces: The chief priests and the scribes stood by, accusing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} fiercely.

L.10: And the chief priests and the scribes stood [there], vehemently accusing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.10: The chief priests and the teachers of the law were standing there. They kept making strong charges against Jesus.

decisions.choice: vehemently: with force and intensity
decisions.reason: The adverb describes doing something with all one's strength. Acts 18:28 uses it for Apollos refuting opponents.

decisions.choice: teachers of the law
decisions.reason: Readable says what scribes were, as elsewhere in Luke.

records.source: ἐξουθενήσας δὲ αὐτὸν καὶ ὁ Ἡρῴδης σὺν τοῖς στρατεύμασιν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐμπαίξας περιβαλὼν ἐσθῆτα λαμπρὰν ἀνέπεμψεν αὐτὸν τῷ Πιλάτῳ.
records.gloss: Having treated as nothing then him also the Herod with the troops of him and having mocked, having put around [him] clothing bright he sent back him to the Pilate.
pieces: Herod and his soldiers treated {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} with scorn and made fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Herod had {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} dressed in a bright robe and sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} back to Pilate.

L.11: And Herod with his soldiers treated {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} with contempt and mocked [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}], and having put bright clothing on [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}], he sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} back to Pilate.

R.11: Then Herod and his soldiers laughed at Jesus and treated {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} as if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} were worth nothing. They put a shining robe on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, as if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} were a king. Then Herod sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} back to Pilate.

decisions.choice: treated with contempt: treated as nothing
decisions.reason: The verb means to count someone as nothing. It is used in Acts 4:11 of the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22).

decisions.choice: bright clothing: a fine, shining robe put on him in mockery
alternatives: a white robe that showed he was innocent
decisions.reason: The word means bright or splendid. Dressing Jesus in a king's finery mocks his claim to be a king. Some think the robe also showed that Herod found him innocent, but Luke does not say so.

decisions.choice: troops: the soldiers of Herod's guard
decisions.reason: Herod had his own soldiers; the Roman soldiers mock Jesus later (23:36).

decisions.choice: as if he were a king
decisions.reason: Readable explains why the robe was mockery. The point is clear from the charge (23:2-3), but Luke does not spell it out.

records.source: ἐγένοντο δὲ φίλοι ὅ τε Ἡρῴδης καὶ ὁ Πιλᾶτος ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ μετ’ ἀλλήλων· προϋπῆρχον γὰρ ἐν ἔχθρᾳ ὄντες πρὸς αὑτούς.
records.gloss: Became then friends the both Herod and the Pilate on very the day with one another; were before for in enmity being toward themselves.
pieces: That same day Herod and Pilate became friends. Until then there had been hostility between them.

L.12: And both Herod and Pilate became friends with one another on that very day, for before [this] they had been at enmity with each other.

R.12: Herod and Pilate had been enemies before. But on that day they became friends.

decisions.choice: they had been at enmity: the cause is not told
decisions.reason: Luke does not say why they were enemies. Pilate's killing of some Galileans (13:1) may have offended Herod, who ruled Galilee, but that is a guess.

decisions.choice: Herod and Pilate became friends: rulers joined against the Lord's anointed
alternatives: a detail of no further meaning
decisions.reason: In Acts 4:25-27 the believers pray Psalm 2:1-2 and see it fulfilled when Herod and Pontius Pilate gathered against Jesus.

decisions.choice: the earlier enmity first
decisions.reason: Readable tells the events in the order they happened.

records.source: Πιλᾶτος δὲ συγκαλεσάμενος τοὺς ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ τοὺς ἄρχοντας καὶ τὸν λαὸν εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Προσηνέγκατέ μοι τὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦτον ὡς ἀποστρέφοντα τὸν λαόν, καὶ ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἐνώπιον ὑμῶν ἀνακρίνας οὐθὲν εὗρον ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τούτῳ αἴτιον ὧν κατηγορεῖτε κατ’ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Pilate then having called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people \v 14 said to them, You brought to me the man this as turning away the people, and behold I before you having examined nothing found in the man this guilt of which you accuse against him.
pieces: Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers and the people

and said to them, "You brought this man before me on the charge that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was turning the people from their loyalty. I have questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in your presence, and I have found {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} guilty of none of the things you accuse {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} of.

L.13: And Pilate called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people
L.14: and said to them, "You brought this man to me as one who turns the people away, and look, having examined [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] before you, I have found in this man no guilt of the things of which you accuse {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.13: Pilate called together the chief priests, the other leaders and the people.
R.14: He said to them, "You brought this man to me. You said that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was getting the people to rebel. I have questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} here in front of you. But I have not found {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} guilty of any of the things you say {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did.

decisions.choice: turning the people away: inciting them to revolt
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn someone away, here from loyalty to their rulers. It sums up the charges of 23:2 and 23:5 with a different word.

decisions.choice: the second time Pilate declares Jesus innocent
decisions.reason: Pilate repeats the verdict of 23:4, now after a hearing in their presence (23:22 gives the third).

decisions.choice: the rulers: members of the council
decisions.reason: The same rulers appear at the cross (23:35) and in 24:20, where the two from Emmaus say that their rulers handed Jesus over.

decisions.choice: the people: now called in with their leaders
decisions.reason: Until now the people had been on Jesus' side, and the leaders feared them (20:19; 22:2). Here they are gathered with the leaders.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Pilate uses this word to point to his own verdict. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: getting the people to rebel
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of turning away was charged, as 23:2 and 23:5 show.

records.source: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ Ἡρῴδης, ἀνέπεμψεν γὰρ αὐτὸν πρὸς ἡμᾶς· καὶ ἰδοὺ οὐδὲν ἄξιον θανάτου ἐστὶν πεπραγμένον αὐτῷ·
records.gloss: But not even Herod, he sent back for him to us; and behold nothing worthy of death is having been done by him;
pieces: Neither did Herod, for he sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} back to us. Plainly {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has done nothing that deserves death.

L.15: Neither [did] Herod, for he sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} back to us; and look, nothing deserving death has been done by {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.15: Herod did not find {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} guilty either. That is why he sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} back to us. This man has done nothing that deserves the death penalty.

decisions.choice: he sent him back to us: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: I sent you to him, the reading of many manuscripts
decisions.reason: The early papyrus P75, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus read "he sent him back to us". Many other manuscripts, Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Bezae among them, read "I sent you to him". The meaning is much the same: Herod too found nothing. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: nothing worthy of death: no crime that carries the death penalty
decisions.reason: The phrase is a legal one. Paul's case is described in the same words in Acts 23:29 and 26:31.

decisions.choice: the sentence runs on into 23:16
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the verse with a raised dot; Pilate's conclusion follows in the next sentence.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Pilate uses this word to stress his conclusion. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: Herod did not find him guilty either
decisions.reason: Readable supplies what Herod did not do, which the Greek leaves to be understood from 23:14.

records.source: παιδεύσας οὖν αὐτὸν ἀπολύσω.
records.gloss: Having punished therefore him I will release [him].
pieces: So I will have {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} flogged and then let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} go."

L.16: Therefore I will punish {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and release [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}]."

R.16: So I will have {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} whipped, and then I will let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} go free."

decisions.choice: punish: a beating as a warning, short of death
alternatives: the scourging that came before crucifixion
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to train or discipline. Here it is a lighter beating meant to teach a lesson, offered so that Jesus could then be released.

decisions.choice: no verse 17: the SBLGNT has no verse here
alternatives: verse 17, "Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the feast", found in many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add a sentence saying that Pilate had to release one prisoner at the feast; Codex Bezae has it after 23:19 instead. It is missing from the early papyrus P75 and from Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Vaticanus, and its changing position suggests it was added from Mark 15:6 or Matthew 27:15. The verse number is therefore skipped, and the text goes on at 23:18. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: have him flogged (B); have him whipped (R)
decisions.reason: A governor would order soldiers to do the beating; Balanced and Readable say what kind of punishment was meant.

records.source: Ἀνέκραγον δὲ παμπληθεὶ λέγοντες· Αἶρε τοῦτον, ἀπόλυσον δὲ ἡμῖν τὸν Βαραββᾶν·
records.gloss: They cried out however all together saying, Take away this [man], release now to us the Barabbas;
pieces: But the whole crowd shouted as one, "Take this man away! Set Barabbas free for us!"

L.18: But they all cried out together, saying, "Away with this man, and release Barabbas to us!"

R.18: But the whole crowd shouted together, "Kill this man! Let Barabbas go free for us!"

decisions.choice: Away with this man: a demand that he be put to death
alternatives: send him out of the city
decisions.reason: The verb means to lift up and take away. The crowd in Jerusalem shouts the same words at Paul, adding "from the earth" (Acts 21:36; 22:22).

decisions.choice: Barabbas: a prisoner the crowd wanted freed
decisions.reason: The name is Aramaic for "son of the father". Luke introduces him only here and explains who he was in the next sentence. Because the SBLGNT has no verse 17, Luke does not mention the custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast that the other Gospels describe (Mark 15:6).

decisions.choice: a raised dot: the description of Barabbas follows
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT closes this sentence with a raised dot; the next one is a relative clause about Barabbas.

decisions.choice: Kill
decisions.reason: Readable says what the demand meant, as Acts 22:22 makes clear.

records.heading: The crowd asks for Barabbas

records.source: ὅστις ἦν διὰ στάσιν τινὰ γενομένην ἐν τῇ πόλει καὶ φόνον βληθεὶς ἐν τῇ φυλακῇ.
records.gloss: who was because of an uprising certain having happened in the city and murder having been thrown in the prison.
pieces: He had been put in prison for a riot that broke out in the city, and for murder.

L.19: He was [a man] who had been thrown into prison for a certain uprising that had taken place in the city, and for murder.

R.19: Barabbas was in prison because he had taken part in a revolt in the city. He had also murdered someone.

decisions.choice: uprising: a revolt against the authorities
decisions.reason: The word is used for civil unrest and rebellion (Acts 19:40). The man released was guilty of the very thing Jesus was falsely charged with (23:2, 5, 14).

decisions.choice: who: a relative clause continuing the last sentence
decisions.reason: The Greek describes Barabbas in a clause that hangs on his name in 23:18.

decisions.choice: He was (L); He had (B); Barabbas (R)
decisions.reason: Every level starts a new sentence and supplies a subject.

records.source: πάλιν δὲ ὁ Πιλᾶτος προσεφώνησεν, θέλων ἀπολῦσαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: Again then the Pilate called to [them], wishing to release the Jesus.
pieces: Pilate spoke to them once more, because he wanted to set Jesus free.

L.20: And Pilate called out to [them] again, wishing to release Jesus.

R.20: Pilate wanted to let Jesus go. So he spoke to the crowd again.

decisions.choice: wishing to release Jesus: Pilate's will against theirs
decisions.reason: Luke shows Pilate wanting to release Jesus three times (23:16, 20, 22). In the end he hands Jesus over to their will (23:25).

decisions.choice: his wish first, then his speaking
decisions.reason: Readable states the reason first, which is easier to follow.

records.source: οἱ δὲ ἐπεφώνουν λέγοντες· Σταύρου σταύρου αὐτόν.
records.gloss: They but were shouting saying, Crucify, crucify him.
pieces: But they kept shouting back, "Crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}! Crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}!"

L.21: But they kept shouting, saying, "Crucify, crucify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}!"

R.21: But they kept on shouting, "Nail {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to a cross! Nail {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to a cross!"

decisions.choice: kept shouting ... Crucify, crucify: a continuing, repeated cry
decisions.reason: The verb is imperfect, and the command is present tense and doubled: they shouted it over and over.

decisions.choice: crucify: the Roman death penalty on a cross
decisions.reason: Rome crucified slaves, rebels and violent criminals. The condemned man was nailed or tied to a wooden cross and left to die in public, a death meant to shame.

decisions.choice: Nail him to a cross
decisions.reason: Readable explains what crucifixion was, as in 24:7.

records.source: ὁ δὲ τρίτον εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Τί γὰρ κακὸν ἐποίησεν οὗτος;
records.gloss: The but a third [time] said to them, What for evil did this [man]?
pieces: For the third time he said to them, "Why? What wrong has this man done?

L.22: And a third time he said to them, "Why, what evil has this man done?

R.22: Pilate spoke to them a third time. He said, "Why? What has this man done wrong?

decisions.choice: a third time: Pilate's third verdict of innocence
alternatives: a third speech of any kind
decisions.reason: Luke counts the times: 23:4, 23:14-15 and now here. The repetition makes clear that Jesus was condemned though the judge found him innocent.

decisions.choice: Why: surprise or protest
decisions.reason: The small word in the question expresses surprise: "Why, what has he done?"

decisions.choice: Pilate
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker.

records.source: οὐδὲν αἴτιον θανάτου εὗρον ἐν αὐτῷ· παιδεύσας οὖν αὐτὸν ἀπολύσω.
records.gloss: No cause of death I found in him; having punished therefore him I will release.
pieces: I have found no reason to put {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to death. So I will have {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} flogged and then let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} go."

L.22: I have found in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} no cause for death; therefore I will punish {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and release [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}]."

R.22: I have found nothing that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} should die for. So I will have {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} whipped, and then I will let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} go free."

decisions.choice: cause of death: a crime that deserves the death penalty
decisions.reason: The same legal word as in 23:4 and 23:14, now with "of death": nothing he has done calls for execution.

decisions.choice: punish: a beating as a warning
alternatives: the scourging that came before crucifixion
decisions.reason: Pilate repeats his offer of 23:16.

decisions.choice: have him flogged (B); have him whipped (R)
decisions.reason: As in 23:16.

records.source: οἱ δὲ ἐπέκειντο φωναῖς μεγάλαις αἰτούμενοι αὐτὸν σταυρωθῆναι, καὶ κατίσχυον αἱ φωναὶ αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: They but were pressing with voices loud asking him to be crucified, and were prevailing the voices of them.
pieces: But they pressed their demand with loud shouts, calling for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to be crucified, and their shouting won the day.

L.23: But they kept pressing [him] with loud voices, demanding that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} be crucified, and their voices prevailed.

R.23: But they kept shouting loudly. They demanded that Jesus be put to death on a cross. In the end their shouting won.

decisions.choice: pressing: insisting, bearing down on Pilate
decisions.reason: The verb means to lie on or press upon. It pictures the crowd pushing Pilate to give way.

decisions.choice: prevailed: overpowered all resistance
decisions.reason: The verb means to be strong enough to win; the same verb is used of the gates of Hades in Matthew 16:18.

decisions.choice: their voices: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: their voices and those of the chief priests, the reading of many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "and those of the chief priests". The early papyrus P75, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus do not have the words. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

records.source: καὶ Πιλᾶτος ἐπέκρινεν γενέσθαι τὸ αἴτημα αὐτῶν·
records.gloss: and Pilate decided to be done the demand of them;
pieces: So Pilate ruled that what they asked for should be done.

L.24: And Pilate gave sentence that their demand be carried out.

R.24: So Pilate decided to give them what they wanted.

decisions.choice: gave sentence: made a formal ruling
decisions.reason: The verb is used for a judge's decision. Pilate acts as judge and decides the case against his own verdict.

decisions.choice: a raised dot: the sentence runs on into 23:25
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT marks a pause here; the next sentence describes what the ruling meant. Every level ends the sentence here.

records.source: ἀπέλυσεν δὲ τὸν διὰ στάσιν καὶ φόνον βεβλημένον εἰς φυλακὴν ὃν ᾐτοῦντο, τὸν δὲ Ἰησοῦν παρέδωκεν τῷ θελήματι αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: He released then the [one] because of uprising and murder having been thrown into prison whom they were asking for, the and Jesus he handed over to the will of them.
pieces: He set free the man they asked for, the one who had been put in prison for revolt and murder. But Jesus he gave up to them to do as they wished.

L.25: And he released the one who had been thrown into prison for uprising and murder, whom they were asking for, but Jesus he handed over to their will.

R.25: He set free the man they wanted, the one who was in prison for rebellion and murder. But he handed Jesus over to them to do whatever they wanted.

decisions.choice: the guilty man released: Luke repeats Barabbas's crimes
decisions.reason: Luke says again why Barabbas was in prison. The rebel and murderer goes free while the innocent one is condemned (Acts 3:14).

decisions.choice: handed over: as Jesus had foretold
decisions.reason: Jesus had said that the Son of Man would be handed over into the hands of men (9:44) and to the Gentiles (18:32). The same verb is used here.

decisions.choice: to their will: to do with him as they wanted
decisions.reason: Pilate gives them what they demand. Roman soldiers carry out the sentence (23:36), but the will that is done is theirs.

records.source: Καὶ ὡς ἀπήγαγον αὐτόν, ἐπιλαβόμενοι Σίμωνά τινα Κυρηναῖον ἐρχόμενον ἀπ’ ἀγροῦ ἐπέθηκαν αὐτῷ τὸν σταυρὸν φέρειν ὄπισθεν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: And as they led away him, having seized Simon a certain Cyrenian coming from [the] country they put on him the cross to carry behind the Jesus.
pieces: As they led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away, they took hold of a man named Simon from Cyrene, who was coming in from the countryside. They laid the cross on him and made him carry it behind Jesus.

L.26: And as they led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away, they seized a certain Simon, a Cyrenian, coming from the country, and put the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.

R.26: The soldiers led Jesus away. On the way they grabbed a man named Simon, from the city of Cyrene in Africa. He was coming into Jerusalem from the fields. They put the cross on him and made him carry it behind Jesus.

decisions.choice: a Cyrenian: from Cyrene in North Africa
decisions.reason: Cyrene was a city in what is now Libya, with a large Jewish community; Jews from Cyrene were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10; 6:9). Mark 15:21 names Simon's sons, Alexander and Rufus.

decisions.choice: they seized him and put the cross on him
decisions.reason: A condemned man usually carried his own cross, or its crossbeam, to the place of execution. Roman soldiers could force a passer-by to carry a load (Matthew 5:41).

decisions.choice: to carry behind Jesus: the picture of a disciple
alternatives: only a note of the order of the procession
decisions.reason: Luke's wording recalls Jesus' call to take up one's cross and come after him (9:23; 14:27).

decisions.choice: the country: the fields outside the city
alternatives: his farm, where he had been working
decisions.reason: The word means the countryside. Luke does not say why Simon had been there.

decisions.choice: The soldiers
decisions.reason: Readable names who led Jesus away; Luke mentions the soldiers in 23:36.

records.heading: On the way to the Skull

records.source: Ἠκολούθει δὲ αὐτῷ πολὺ πλῆθος τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ γυναικῶν αἳ ἐκόπτοντο καὶ ἐθρήνουν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Were following now him a great multitude of the people and of women who were beating themselves and lamenting him.
pieces: A large crowd of the people followed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, among them women who were mourning and wailing for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.27: And a great multitude of the people followed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and of women who were beating their breasts and lamenting for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.27: A large crowd of people followed Jesus. Among them were women who were crying and beating their chests in sorrow for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: beating their breasts and lamenting: the public mourning for the dead
decisions.reason: Mourners struck their chests and wailed aloud, as at the death of Jairus's daughter (8:52). The women mourn Jesus as one already dead.

decisions.choice: a great multitude of the people: the people are not all against him
alternatives: the crowd that shouted for his death
decisions.reason: Luke sets the people who follow and mourn beside the leaders who condemn. At the cross the people watch while the rulers mock (23:35), and the crowds go home grieving (23:48).

decisions.choice: mourning
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the general word for the act of mourning; Literal and Readable show the gesture.

records.source: στραφεὶς δὲ πρὸς αὐτὰς ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν· Θυγατέρες Ἰερουσαλήμ, μὴ κλαίετε ἐπ’ ἐμέ· πλὴν ἐφ’ ἑαυτὰς κλαίετε καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν, ὅτι ἰδοὺ ἔρχονται ἡμέραι ἐν αἷς ἐροῦσιν Μακάριαι αἱ στεῖραι καὶ αἱ κοιλίαι αἳ οὐκ ἐγέννησαν καὶ μαστοὶ οἳ οὐκ ἔθρεψαν.
records.gloss: Having turned then to them the Jesus said, Daughters of Jerusalem, not weep for me; but for yourselves weep and for the children of you, \v 29 for behold are coming days in which they will say, Blessed the barren and the wombs that not bore and breasts that not nursed.
pieces: Jesus turned toward them and said, "Daughters of Jerusalem, it is not {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} you should be weeping over. Weep over yourselves and over your children.
Days are coming when people will say, 'Blessed are the women who could not have children, the wombs that never gave birth and the breasts that never fed a baby.'

L.28: And Jesus turned to them and said, "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; rather weep for yourselves and for your children,
L.29: for look, days are coming in which they will say, 'Blessed [are] the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not nurse.'

R.28: Jesus turned to the women and said, "Women of Jerusalem, do not cry for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. Cry for yourselves and for your children.
R.29: A time is coming when people will say, 'Blessed are the women who never had children. Blessed are those who never gave birth and never fed a baby at the breast.'

decisions.choice: Daughters of Jerusalem: the women of the city
decisions.reason: The phrase is a way of addressing the women as belonging to the city, as Scripture speaks of the daughter of Zion (Zechariah 9:9). What he says is about Jerusalem as a whole.

decisions.choice: days are coming: the coming disaster for Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Jesus had wept over the city and foretold its destruction (19:41-44), and had said how hard those days would be for women who were pregnant or nursing (21:20-24).

decisions.choice: blessed are the barren: a reversal of what is normally said
alternatives: a blessing on not having children in general
decisions.reason: To be childless was usually a grief (1:25). In the coming disaster it would be better to have no children to watch suffer.

decisions.choice: they will say: people in general
alternatives: the women he is speaking to
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject; it means what people will be saying in those days.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Jesus uses this word to draw attention to the warning. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: Women of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom.

records.source: τότε ἄρξονται λέγειν τοῖς ὄρεσιν· Πέσετε ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς, καὶ τοῖς βουνοῖς· Καλύψατε ἡμᾶς·
records.gloss: Then they will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us;
pieces: Then they will start saying to the mountains, 'Fall on us!' and to the hills, 'Cover us!'

L.30: Then they will begin to say to the mountains, 'Fall on us,' and to the hills, 'Cover us.'

R.30: People will call out to the mountains, 'Fall on us!' They will cry to the hills, 'Cover us up!'

decisions.choice: the words of Hosea 10:8
decisions.reason: Hosea foretold that when judgment came on Samaria, people would beg the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them. Revelation 6:16 uses the same words.

decisions.choice: Fall on us ... Cover us: a wish to die rather than face what is coming
decisions.reason: The cry asks for death, or to be hidden from the judgment, because it is too terrible to bear.

decisions.choice: a raised dot: the reason follows in 23:31
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT marks a pause; Jesus' explanation follows in the next sentence.

records.source: ὅτι εἰ ἐν τῷ ὑγρῷ ξύλῳ ταῦτα ποιοῦσιν, ἐν τῷ ξηρῷ τί γένηται;
records.gloss: For if in the green wood these things they do, in the dry what may happen?
pieces: For if this is how they treat wood that is green, what will become of wood that is dry?"

L.31: For if they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?"

R.31: If this is what they do to a tree that is green and growing, what will happen to a tree that is dry?"

decisions.choice: green wood and dry: if the innocent suffers like this, the guilty will suffer far worse
alternatives: if the Romans treat Jesus so, they will treat the rebel city worse
if the people do this now, what will they do later
decisions.reason: Green wood does not burn easily; dry wood is ready for the fire. The saying most likely means: if Jesus, who has done nothing wrong, meets such a fate, what will come on Jerusalem, which is ripe for judgment? Ezekiel 20:47 (21:3 in the Hebrew numbering) speaks of a fire that burns up every green tree and every dry tree. The proverb can be read in more than one way.

decisions.choice: they do: unclear who is meant
alternatives: a way of speaking of God's judgment
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject. It may be the Romans who carry out the sentence, the leaders who demanded it, or simply people in general. Every level keeps "they".

decisions.choice: a tree that is green and growing
decisions.reason: Readable makes the picture clear: a living tree as against dry, dead wood.

records.source: Ἤγοντο δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι κακοῦργοι δύο σὺν αὐτῷ ἀναιρεθῆναι.
records.gloss: Were being led now also others criminals two with him to be put to death.
pieces: Two other men, both criminals, were also led out with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to be executed.

L.32: And two others, criminals, were also being led away with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to be put to death.

R.32: Two other men were also being taken out to be killed with Jesus. They were criminals.

decisions.choice: two others, criminals: Jesus is not called a criminal
alternatives: two other criminals, as if Jesus were one too
decisions.reason: The Greek can be read word by word as "other criminals, two", but the sense is "two others, who were criminals". Every level avoids suggesting that Jesus was one of them.

decisions.choice: with him: counted among the lawless
decisions.reason: At the supper Jesus quoted Isaiah 53:12, that he would be counted with the lawless, and said it must be fulfilled in him (22:37).

decisions.choice: criminals: those who do evil
decisions.reason: The word means evildoers. Mark 15:27 uses a word for bandits or rebels.

records.source: καὶ ὅτε ἦλθον ἐπὶ τὸν τόπον τὸν καλούμενον Κρανίον, ἐκεῖ ἐσταύρωσαν αὐτὸν καὶ τοὺς κακούργους, ὃν μὲν ἐκ δεξιῶν ὃν δὲ ἐξ ἀριστερῶν.
records.gloss: And when they came to the place the [one] called Skull, there they crucified him and the criminals, one on [the] right one and on [the] left.
pieces: When they reached the place called the Skull, they crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} there, with the criminals, one at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand and one at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

L.33: And when they came to the place called "Skull," there they crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and the criminals, one on [the] right and one on [the] left.

R.33: They came to a place called The Skull. There the soldiers nailed Jesus to a cross. They also nailed the two criminals to crosses, one on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right side and one on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

decisions.choice: Skull: the place of execution outside the city
decisions.reason: Mark 15:22 and John 19:17 give its Aramaic name, Golgotha, which means skull; the Latin word for skull gave the name Calvary. Why it was so called is not known. It was outside the city wall (John 19:20; Hebrews 13:12).

decisions.choice: they crucified him: Luke tells it in a single word
decisions.reason: Luke does not describe the nailing or the suffering. The bare word says all that his readers needed to know.

decisions.choice: one on the right and one on the left: Jesus in the middle
alternatives: a detail of no further meaning
decisions.reason: Placed between two criminals, Jesus is counted with the lawless, as he had said (22:37; Isaiah 53:12).

decisions.choice: his right ... his left
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose right and left is meant.

decisions.choice: the soldiers nailed Jesus to a cross
decisions.reason: Readable explains crucifixion and names who did it (23:36).

records.source: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἔλεγεν· Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς, οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν τί ποιοῦσιν.
records.gloss: The and Jesus was saying, Father, forgive them, not for they know what they do.
pieces: Jesus kept saying, "Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing."

L.34: And Jesus was saying, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."

R.34: Jesus said, "Father, forgive these people. They do not understand what they are doing."

decisions.choice: the prayer is included, as in the SBLGNT
alternatives: the prayer is left out, as in several early manuscripts
decisions.reason: The prayer is missing from the early papyrus P75, Codex Vaticanus, the first hand of Codex Bezae, Codex Washingtonianus and the Sinaitic Syriac, and a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus marked it for removal. It is found in the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, in Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi, and in most later manuscripts, and early church writers knew it. It fits Luke's own themes: Stephen prays in the same way as he dies (Acts 7:60), and Peter tells the people of Jerusalem that they acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17). Some think it was left out by copyists who thought the fall of Jerusalem showed the prayer had not been answered; others think it is an old saying of Jesus added here. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: was saying: said, or kept saying
decisions.reason: The verb is imperfect. It may mean that Jesus prayed this more than once, or simply set the scene for his words.

decisions.choice: them: those who were putting him to death
decisions.reason: The word is not limited. It includes the soldiers who were crucifying him and may reach to all who had a part in his death, who acted without knowing what they did (Acts 3:17; 13:27).

decisions.choice: Father: Jesus prays to God as his Father
decisions.reason: Jesus addresses God as Father in prayer (10:21; 22:42) and does so again with his last words (23:46).

records.source: διαμεριζόμενοι δὲ τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ ἔβαλον κλήρους.
records.gloss: Dividing then the garments of him they cast lots.
pieces: They shared out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes among themselves by casting lots.

L.34: And dividing {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes, they cast lots.

R.34: The soldiers divided {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes among themselves. They threw lots to decide who would get each piece.

decisions.choice: dividing his clothes and casting lots: the words of Psalm 22
alternatives: a detail of no further meaning
decisions.reason: Psalm 22:19 says of the sufferer, "they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." John 19:24 names the psalm.

decisions.choice: casting lots: deciding by chance
decisions.reason: Lots were marked stones or pieces of wood shaken out, much like dice. The clothes of an executed man went to those who carried out the sentence.

decisions.choice: The soldiers
decisions.reason: Readable names who divided the clothes; Luke mentions them in 23:36.

records.source: καὶ εἱστήκει ὁ λαὸς θεωρῶν.
records.gloss: And stood the people watching.
pieces: The people stood there looking on.

R.35: The people stood there and watched.

decisions.choice: watching: looking on as at a spectacle
decisions.reason: The verb means to look at or watch. Luke does not say that the people mocked; he keeps the mocking for the rulers, the soldiers and one criminal.

decisions.choice: the people stood watching: those who see the sufferer in Psalm 22
alternatives: a detail of no further meaning
decisions.reason: Psalm 22:8 speaks of all who see the sufferer and sneer at him. Luke uses the verbs of that verse here and in the next sentence.

records.source: ἐξεμυκτήριζον δὲ καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες λέγοντες· Ἄλλους ἔσωσεν, σωσάτω ἑαυτόν, εἰ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ χριστὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἐκλεκτός.
records.gloss: Were sneering then also the rulers saying, Others he saved, let him save himself, if this is the Christ of the God, the chosen.
pieces: The rulers joined in the scoffing. "He saved others," they said. "So let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} save {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, if this man is God's {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, the one God chose."

L.35: And the rulers also were sneering, saying, "He saved others; let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} save {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, if this is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} of God, the Chosen One."

R.35: The leaders laughed at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} too. They said, "He saved other people. Let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} save {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} now, if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} really is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} whom God sent, the one God has chosen!"

decisions.choice: sneering: turning up the nose in scorn
decisions.reason: The verb pictures a sneer of contempt. It is the verb of the Greek version of Psalm 22:8, where those who see the sufferer sneer at him.

decisions.choice: He saved others; let him save himself: mockery that says more than it means
decisions.reason: Jesus had saved others: he healed the sick and forgave sinners, and came to seek and to save the lost (7:50; 19:10). The rulers think that one who cannot save himself cannot be the Christ; Luke's readers know that he saves others by not saving himself.

decisions.choice: the Christ of God, the Chosen One: God's anointed King, the one he has chosen
decisions.reason: Peter called Jesus "the Christ of God" (9:20), and the voice from the cloud called him "my Son, the chosen one" (9:35), recalling God's chosen servant of Isaiah 42:1. The rulers use the titles to mock him.

decisions.choice: this: said with contempt
decisions.reason: The rulers do not name Jesus; "this one" keeps him at a distance.

decisions.choice: they said
decisions.reason: Balanced places the speaker words inside the quotation, which reads more naturally.

decisions.choice: God's Christ / the Christ of God, with Messiah as the alternative
decisions.reason: The title follows the christos setting; Balanced uses the possessive form as at 9:20.

records.source: ἐνέπαιξαν δὲ αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ στρατιῶται προσερχόμενοι, ὄξος προσφέροντες αὐτῷ καὶ λέγοντες· Εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων, σῶσον σεαυτόν.
records.gloss: Mocked then him also the soldiers coming near, sour wine offering him \v 37 and saying, If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself.
pieces: The soldiers made fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} as well. They came up and held out sour wine to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}},
saying, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the king of the Jews, save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}!"

L.36: And the soldiers also mocked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, coming up [and] offering {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} sour wine
L.37: and saying, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the king of the Jews, save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}!"

R.36: The soldiers made fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} too. They came close and offered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} some cheap sour wine.
R.37: They said, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the king of the Jews, then save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}!"

decisions.choice: sour wine: the cheap, vinegary wine soldiers drank
decisions.reason: The word is for wine that has turned sour, a common drink of soldiers and laborers. Here it is offered in mockery.

decisions.choice: offering him sour wine: the words of Psalm 69
decisions.reason: Psalm 69:22 says of the sufferer, "for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink."

decisions.choice: If you are: said in scorn
decisions.reason: The soldiers assume he is not a king. The words echo the devil's "If you are the Son of God" (4:3, 9).

decisions.choice: cheap sour wine
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of drink this was.

records.source: ἦν δὲ καὶ ἐπιγραφὴ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ· Ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων οὗτος.
records.gloss: There was now also an inscription over him, The king of the Jews this.
pieces: Above {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} there was also a written notice: "This is the king of the Jews."

L.38: And there was also an inscription over {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "This [is] the king of the Jews."

R.38: A notice had been put up above {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head. It said, "This is the king of the Jews."

decisions.choice: an inscription: the charge written on a board
decisions.reason: The charge against a condemned man was written on a board and carried before him or fixed to the cross, so that all could read why he died (John 19:19-20).

decisions.choice: an inscription over him: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: an inscription written over him in Greek, Latin and Hebrew letters, the reading of many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add that the notice was written in Greek, Latin and Hebrew, words probably taken from John 19:20. The early papyrus P75, Codex Vaticanus and others do not have them. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the king of the Jews: a mocking charge that states the truth
decisions.reason: The notice was meant to mock and to warn, but Luke's readers know that Jesus is the King promised to sit on David's throne (1:32-33; 19:38).

decisions.choice: above his head
decisions.reason: Readable says where the notice was placed.

records.source: Εἷς δὲ τῶν κρεμασθέντων κακούργων ἐβλασφήμει αὐτόν λέγων· Οὐχὶ σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστός;
records.gloss: One now of the having been hanged criminals was insulting him saying, Not you are the Christ?
pieces: One of the criminals hanging beside {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} kept abusing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. "You are the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not?

L.39: And one of the criminals who had been hanged [there] kept insulting {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?

R.39: One of the criminals hanging there began to say cruel things to Jesus. He said, "You are the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not?

decisions.choice: insulting: speaking abusively, reviling
decisions.reason: The verb is the one from which "blaspheme" comes. Spoken against a person it means to insult or revile; Luke uses it of the guards who mocked Jesus (22:65).

decisions.choice: Are you not the Christ: a question that expects yes, said in scorn
decisions.reason: The form of the question expects agreement, but the man means it as a taunt, as the demand that follows shows.

decisions.choice: hanged: hanging on a cross
decisions.reason: Crucifixion could be spoken of as hanging on a tree (Acts 5:30; 10:39; Galatians 3:13, recalling Deuteronomy 21:23).

decisions.choice: You are the Christ, are you not?
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the expected answer plain.

records.heading: The two criminals

records.source: σῶσον σεαυτὸν καὶ ἡμᾶς.
records.gloss: Save yourself and us.
pieces: Then save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}, and us too!"

R.39: Then save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}, and save us too!"

decisions.choice: Save yourself: the third time the taunt is heard
decisions.reason: The rulers (23:35), the soldiers (23:37) and now a criminal all call on Jesus to save himself. He is the Savior (2:11), but he does not use his power for himself.

decisions.choice: Then
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable link the demand to the question before it.

records.source: ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ ἕτερος ἐπιτιμῶν αὐτῷ ἔφη· Οὐδὲ φοβῇ σὺ τὸν θεόν, ὅτι ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ κρίματι εἶ;
records.gloss: Answering now the other rebuking him said, Not even fear you the God, that in the same sentence you are?
pieces: But the other criminal rebuked him: "Have you no fear even of God, when you are under the same sentence of death?

L.40: But the other answered, and rebuking him said, "Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same sentence?

R.40: But the other criminal told him he was wrong. He said, "You should be afraid of God! You are being punished with the same death as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is.

decisions.choice: not even: you, of all people, should fear God
alternatives: you do not fear God either, like the mockers
decisions.reason: The word may mean that he does not even fear God, let alone respect Jesus; or that, facing death himself, he ought at least to fear God.

decisions.choice: sentence: the condemnation to death
decisions.reason: The word is for a judge's verdict. All three men are under the same sentence of crucifixion.

decisions.choice: since: the reason he should fear God
decisions.reason: The small word gives the reason: being under the same sentence, he is close to standing before God.

decisions.choice: You should be afraid of God!
alternatives: Do you not even fear God?
decisions.reason: Readable turns the rebuking question into a statement.

decisions.choice: as he is
decisions.reason: Readable says who else is under the sentence.

records.source: καὶ ἡμεῖς μὲν δικαίως, ἄξια γὰρ ὧν ἐπράξαμεν ἀπολαμβάνομεν· οὗτος δὲ οὐδὲν ἄτοπον ἔπραξεν.
records.gloss: and we indeed justly, worthy for of what we did we are receiving; this [man] however nothing out of place did.
pieces: For us it is fair: we are paying the due price for what we did. But this man has done nothing amiss."

L.41: And we indeed [are suffering] justly, for we are receiving what is deserved for what we did; but this man has done nothing out of place."

R.41: We deserve to be punished. We are getting what we earned by the things we did. But this man has not done anything wrong."

decisions.choice: out of place: improper, wrong in any way
alternatives: only no crime worthy of death
decisions.reason: The word means out of place or unfitting. The criminal says more than that Jesus is innocent of the charge: he has done nothing wrong at all.

decisions.choice: this man did nothing wrong: another witness to his innocence
decisions.reason: Pilate (23:4, 14, 22), Herod (23:15), this criminal and the centurion (23:47) all speak of Jesus as innocent.

decisions.choice: justly: rightly, as the law requires
decisions.reason: The adverb is formed from the word the centurion uses of Jesus in 23:47: the criminals suffer justly, but Jesus is just.

decisions.choice: [are suffering]
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the verb to be understood; Literal supplies it in brackets.

records.source: καὶ ἔλεγεν· Ἰησοῦ, μνήσθητί μου ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σου.
records.gloss: And he was saying, Jesus, remember me when you come in the kingdom of you.
pieces: Then he said, "Jesus, remember me when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} come in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} kingdom."

L.42: And he was saying, "Jesus, remember me when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} come in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} kingdom."

R.42: Then he said, "Jesus, please remember me when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} come as king."

decisions.choice: in your kingdom: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: into your kingdom, the reading of the early papyrus P75 and Codex Vaticanus
decisions.reason: Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi and most later manuscripts read "in your kingdom", that is, when Jesus comes in royal power (9:26). P75 and Codex Vaticanus read "into your kingdom", when he enters his reign (compare 24:26). Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: remember me: think of me with favor and act for me
decisions.reason: In Scripture to ask someone to remember you is to ask for their help (Genesis 40:14; 1 Samuel 1:11; Psalm 106:4).

decisions.choice: when you come in your kingdom: the criminal believes that Jesus is a king
decisions.reason: Where the others mock the title on the notice, this man trusts that Jesus will reign after his death.

decisions.choice: when you come as king
alternatives: when you come in your kingdom
decisions.reason: Readable says what coming in his kingdom means.

records.source: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἀμήν σοι λέγω σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.
records.gloss: And he said to him, Truly to you I say today with me you will be in the paradise.
pieces: Jesus answered him, "Truly I tell you, this very day you will be with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in paradise."

L.43: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to him, "Truly I tell you, today you will be with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in paradise."

R.43: Jesus answered him, "I tell you the truth: before this day is over, you will be with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in paradise."

decisions.choice: today goes with what follows: today you will be with me
alternatives: I tell you today: you will be with me
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has no comma here. Jesus' sayings that begin "Truly I tell you" do not add "today" to the opening words, and Luke often uses "today" for salvation that comes now (2:11; 4:21; 19:9).

decisions.choice: paradise: the place of the righteous dead with God
decisions.reason: The word, from Persian, means a garden or park. The Greek version of the Old Testament used it for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8), and it came to mean the place where God's people are with him (2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7).

decisions.choice: today ... with me: more than the man asked
decisions.reason: He asked to be remembered when Jesus comes as king. Jesus promises that he will be with him that same day.

decisions.choice: before this day is over
decisions.reason: Readable stresses how soon the promise will come true.

records.source: Καὶ ἦν ἤδη ὡσεὶ ὥρα ἕκτη καὶ σκότος ἐγένετο ἐφ’ ὅλην τὴν γῆν ἕως ὥρας ἐνάτης τοῦ ἡλίου ἐκλιπόντος, ἐσχίσθη δὲ τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ μέσον.
records.gloss: And it was already about [the] hour sixth, and darkness came over all the land until [the] hour ninth, \v 45 the sun having failed, was torn then the curtain of the sanctuary in [the] middle.
pieces: It was already about midday when darkness covered the whole land, and it lasted until three in the afternoon.
The light of the sun failed, and the curtain in the sanctuary was torn down the middle.

L.44: And it was already about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour,
L.45: the sun['s light] having failed; and the curtain of the sanctuary was torn in the middle.

R.44: It was now about the middle of the day. Then the whole land became dark, and it stayed dark until three in the afternoon.
R.45: The sun's light failed. And the heavy curtain in the temple was torn right down the middle.

decisions.choice: the sixth hour to the ninth: from about noon to about three in the afternoon
alternatives: six and nine in the morning
decisions.reason: Hours were counted from sunrise, at about six in the morning.

decisions.choice: the land: the land of Israel
decisions.reason: The word can mean land or earth. Luke may mean only the land around Jerusalem, or the whole world.

decisions.choice: the sun having failed: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: the sun was darkened, the reading of many manuscripts
decisions.reason: The early papyrus P75, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus read "the sun having failed". Many later manuscripts read "and the sun was darkened". The verb of the earlier reading can be used of an eclipse, but a solar eclipse cannot happen at Passover, which fell at full moon, nor last three hours; it may be the plain sense, that the sun's light failed, which every level gives. Some think copyists changed the word to avoid the idea of an eclipse. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the curtain of the sanctuary: a curtain in the temple building itself
alternatives: a curtain in the outer courts
decisions.reason: The sanctuary was the building that held the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place. A curtain separated the two (Exodus 26:31-33), and another hung at its entrance; Luke does not say which. Hebrews 10:19-20 speaks of the way into God's presence opened through Jesus' flesh, as through the curtain.

decisions.choice: darkness at midday: a sign of God's judgment
decisions.reason: Amos 8:9 speaks of a day when God would make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight.

decisions.choice: midday ... three in the afternoon
alternatives: the sixth hour ... the ninth hour
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the time as readers count it today.

decisions.choice: the temple
decisions.reason: Readable uses the more familiar word.

records.heading: Darkness at midday and Jesus' last words

records.source: καὶ φωνήσας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν· Πάτερ, εἰς χεῖράς σου παρατίθεμαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου.
records.gloss: And having called out with a voice loud the Jesus said, Father, into hands of you I entrust the spirit of me.
pieces: Then Jesus cried out in a loud voice, "Father, I place {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} spirit in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hands."

L.46: And Jesus called out with a loud voice and said, "Father, into {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hands I entrust {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} spirit."

R.46: Then Jesus shouted, "Father, I give {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} spirit into {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} care!"

decisions.choice: into your hands I entrust my spirit: the words of Psalm 31
decisions.reason: The prayer is Psalm 31:6, the prayer of one who trusts God when enemies surround him. Jesus adds "Father".

decisions.choice: entrust: hand over for safekeeping
decisions.reason: The verb is used for placing something in someone's care (12:48; Acts 20:32). Jesus dies trusting his Father.

decisions.choice: spirit: his life, his very self
decisions.reason: At death the spirit leaves the body (8:55). Stephen prays in the same way as he dies (Acts 7:59).

decisions.choice: a loud voice: a strong cry, not a faint whisper
decisions.reason: Mark 15:37 also tells of a loud cry at the moment of death.

decisions.choice: into your care
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ εἰπὼν ἐξέπνευσεν.
records.gloss: This then having said he breathed out.
pieces: With these words {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} breathed out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} last breath.

L.46: And having said this, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} breathed out [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}} last].

decisions.choice: breathed out: died
decisions.reason: The verb means to breathe out, a gentle way of saying that someone died (Mark 15:37). It is related to the word for spirit in the prayer just spoken.

decisions.choice: died
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the idiom means.

records.source: Ἰδὼν δὲ ὁ ἑκατοντάρχης τὸ γενόμενον ἐδόξαζεν τὸν θεὸν λέγων· Ὄντως ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος δίκαιος ἦν.
records.gloss: Having seen then the centurion that having happened he was glorifying the God saying, Certainly the man this righteous was.
pieces: The centurion saw what had taken place, and he gave glory to God, saying, "Truly this man was righteous."

L.47: And when the centurion saw what had happened, he began glorifying God, saying, "Certainly this man was righteous."

R.47: The Roman army officer saw what had happened. He gave glory to God and said, "This man really was righteous. He had done nothing wrong!"

decisions.choice: the centurion: a Roman officer over about a hundred soldiers
decisions.reason: Centurions commanded the soldiers who carried out executions. Luke speaks well of other centurions (7:2-9; Acts 10:1-2).

decisions.choice: righteous: both innocent of the charge and right before God
alternatives: righteous only, in a religious sense
decisions.reason: The word means just or righteous. After Pilate's verdicts and the criminal's words (23:4, 14, 22, 41), it surely includes "innocent". But Luke uses the same word for people who are right with God (1:6; 2:25; 23:50), and in Acts Jesus is called "the Righteous One" (Acts 3:14; 7:52; 22:14), recalling the righteous servant of Isaiah 53:11. Where Mark 15:39 and Matthew 27:54 have "Son of God", Luke gives this word.

decisions.choice: glorifying God: praise even at Jesus' death
decisions.reason: In Luke people often glorify God when they see what Jesus does (5:25; 7:16; 13:13; 18:43). Here a Gentile soldier does so when he sees how Jesus died.

decisions.choice: he began glorifying: the imperfect tense
decisions.reason: The tense describes an action begun and continued.

decisions.choice: gave glory to God
decisions.reason: The key term is kept with the noun "glory", which reads more naturally than "glorified".

decisions.choice: He had done nothing wrong!
decisions.reason: Readable adds the sense of innocence that the word carries in this setting, as the criminal said in 23:41.

decisions.choice: The Roman army officer
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a centurion was.

records.source: καὶ πάντες οἱ συμπαραγενόμενοι ὄχλοι ἐπὶ τὴν θεωρίαν ταύτην, θεωρήσαντες τὰ γενόμενα, τύπτοντες τὰ στήθη ὑπέστρεφον.
records.gloss: And all the having come together crowds to the spectacle this, having seen the things having happened, beating the breasts were returning.
pieces: All the crowds who had gathered to watch this spectacle saw what had happened, and they turned back home, striking their breasts.

L.48: And all the crowds who had come together for this spectacle, having seen the things that had happened, were returning, beating [their] breasts.

R.48: Large crowds had come to watch. When they saw what happened, they beat their chests in sorrow as they went home.

decisions.choice: beating their breasts: a sign of grief and sorrow for sin
decisions.reason: The tax collector in the temple beat his breast as he prayed for mercy (18:13). The crowds who came to watch go home grieving.

decisions.choice: spectacle: a public sight that people come to watch
decisions.reason: The word is used for a show or public event. The crowds came to look, as at an execution, and went away changed.

decisions.choice: the crowds' grief: a first turning
decisions.reason: The people who had been gathered against Jesus now mourn. In Acts many in Jerusalem are cut to the heart when they hear what they have done (Acts 2:37).

decisions.choice: in sorrow
decisions.reason: Readable says what the gesture meant.

records.source: εἱστήκεισαν δὲ πάντες οἱ γνωστοὶ αὐτῷ μακρόθεν, καὶ γυναῖκες αἱ συνακολουθοῦσαι αὐτῷ ἀπὸ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, ὁρῶσαι ταῦτα.
records.gloss: Stood then all the knowing him from afar, and women the having followed with him from the Galilee, seeing these things.
pieces: Everyone who knew {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} stood far off. The women who had come with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} from Galilee were standing there too, and they saw these things.

L.49: And all those who knew {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} stood at a distance, and [the] women who had followed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} from Galilee, seeing these things.

R.49: All of Jesus' friends were standing far away. The women who had followed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} from Galilee were there too. They watched everything that happened.

decisions.choice: standing at a distance: the friends of the sufferer
alternatives: a detail of no further meaning
decisions.reason: Psalm 38:12 speaks of the sufferer's friends and neighbors who stand far off.

decisions.choice: those who knew him: his friends and acquaintances
decisions.reason: The word means people known to someone. It may include the apostles and other disciples.

decisions.choice: seeing: the women are the ones who saw
decisions.reason: The participle is feminine. Luke stresses that the women saw what happened; they will see the burial (23:55) and find the tomb empty (24:1-10).

decisions.choice: the women from Galilee: those who had followed and supported Jesus
decisions.reason: Luke has named some of them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others (8:2-3; 24:10).

decisions.choice: Jesus' friends
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plain word for those who knew him.

records.source: Καὶ ἰδοὺ ἀνὴρ ὀνόματι Ἰωσὴφ βουλευτὴς ὑπάρχων, ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ δίκαιος οὗτος οὐκ ἦν συγκατατεθειμένος τῇ βουλῇ καὶ τῇ πράξει αὐτῶν ἀπὸ Ἁριμαθαίας πόλεως τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ὃς προσεδέχετο τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ, οὗτος προσελθὼν τῷ Πιλάτῳ ᾐτήσατο τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, καὶ καθελὼν ἐνετύλιξεν αὐτὸ σινδόνι, καὶ ἔθηκεν αὐτὸν ἐν μνήματι λαξευτῷ οὗ οὐκ ἦν οὐδεὶς οὔπω κείμενος.
records.gloss: And behold a man by name Joseph a council member being, a man good and righteous \v 51 this [one] not was having agreed to the plan and the action of them from Arimathea a city of the Jews, who was waiting for the kingdom of the God, \v 52 this [one] having gone to the Pilate asked [for] the body of the Jesus, \v 53 and having taken down he wrapped it in linen cloth, and placed him in a tomb cut in rock where not was no one not yet lying.
pieces: There was a man named Joseph who was a member of the council, a good and righteous man
who had not given his consent to what the council planned and did. He came from Arimathea, a town of the Jews, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God.
He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
He took the body down from the cross and wrapped it in a linen sheet. Then he laid {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in a tomb cut out of the rock, where no one had ever been buried.

L.50: And look, [there was] a man named Joseph, who was a member of the council, a good and righteous man
L.51: (he had not agreed with their plan and action), from Arimathea, a city of the Jews, who was waiting for the kingdom of God.
L.52: This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus,
L.53: and having taken [it] down, he wrapped it in a linen cloth and placed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in a tomb cut in rock, where no one had ever yet been laid.

R.50: There was a man named Joseph. He was a member of the Jewish council. He was a good man who did what was right in God's eyes.
R.51: He had not agreed with the plan of the other leaders or with what they had done. He came from Arimathea, a Jewish town, and he was waiting for God to set up {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} kingdom.
R.52: Joseph went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
R.53: He took the body down from the cross and wrapped it in a linen cloth. Then he laid {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in a tomb that had been cut out of rock. No one had ever been buried in it before.

decisions.choice: a member of the council: one of the leaders who made up the Jewish council
decisions.reason: The council had condemned Jesus and brought him to Pilate (22:66-23:1). Mark 15:43 calls Joseph a respected member of it.

decisions.choice: righteous: right with God and faithful to his law
decisions.reason: The same word as in 23:47. Luke uses it for Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:6) and Simeon (2:25).

decisions.choice: a remark in the middle of the sentence: he had not agreed
decisions.reason: The clause interrupts the description of Joseph; Literal marks it with parentheses.

decisions.choice: Arimathea: a town of Judea
decisions.reason: Its location is not certain. It is often taken to be Ramathaim, the hometown of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1).

decisions.choice: waiting for the kingdom of God: like the faithful at the start of the Gospel
decisions.reason: Simeon waited for the comfort of Israel and Anna spoke to all who waited for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:25, 38). Joseph shares that hope.

decisions.choice: it ... him: the body, then Jesus himself
decisions.reason: Joseph wraps "it", the body, but lays "him" in the tomb; the second pronoun is masculine and refers to Jesus.

decisions.choice: a linen cloth and a rock-cut tomb where no one had been laid
decisions.reason: Bodies were wrapped in linen and laid in tombs cut into rock. The law said a hanged man's body must not be left overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). A new tomb was fitting for a king; Jesus had entered Jerusalem on a colt no one had ever ridden (19:30).

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to introduce a new person. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: from the cross
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where the body was taken down from.

decisions.choice: a good man who did what was right in God's eyes
decisions.reason: Readable explains what righteous means here.

records.heading: Joseph lays Jesus in a tomb

records.source: καὶ ἡμέρα ἦν παρασκευῆς, καὶ σάββατον ἐπέφωσκεν.
records.gloss: And day it was of preparation, and Sabbath was dawning.
pieces: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was drawing near.

L.54: And it was [the] day of Preparation, and [the] Sabbath was beginning to dawn.

R.54: It was Friday, the day when people got ready for the Sabbath. The Sabbath would begin at sunset.

decisions.choice: the day of Preparation: Friday, the day before the Sabbath
decisions.reason: On Friday people prepared food and everything else they needed, since no work could be done on the Sabbath (Mark 15:42).

decisions.choice: dawning: beginning
decisions.reason: The verb is used for daybreak, but the Sabbath began at sunset on Friday. It may refer to the evening star or the lamps lit as the Sabbath began, or simply mean that it was beginning.

decisions.choice: Friday ... at sunset

records.source: κατακολουθήσασαι δὲ αἱ γυναῖκες, αἵτινες ἦσαν συνεληλυθυῖαι ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας αὐτῷ, ἐθεάσαντο τὸ μνημεῖον καὶ ὡς ἐτέθη τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ, ὑποστρέψασαι δὲ ἡτοίμασαν ἀρώματα καὶ μύρα.
records.gloss: Having followed after then the women, who were having come with out of the Galilee with him, saw the tomb and how was laid the body of him, \v 56 having returned then they prepared spices and perfumed oils.
pieces: The women who had come with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} from Galilee went after Joseph. They saw the tomb and the way {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} body was laid there.
Then they went back and got spices and fragrant oils ready.

L.55: And the women who had come with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out of Galilee followed after and saw the tomb and how {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} body was laid,
L.56: and having returned, they prepared spices and perfumed oils.

R.55: The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed Joseph. They saw the tomb and how Jesus' body was placed in it.
R.56: Then they went home and made sweet-smelling spices and oils to put on the body.

decisions.choice: they saw the tomb: the women are witnesses
decisions.reason: The women saw Jesus die (23:49), saw where and how he was laid, and two days later found the same tomb empty (24:1-3).

decisions.choice: spices and perfumed oils: for the body
decisions.reason: Spices and fragrant oils were put on a body as a last act of love and honor. The women brought them to the tomb on the first day of the week (24:1).

decisions.choice: went after Joseph (B); followed Joseph (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whom they followed.

decisions.choice: to put on the body
decisions.reason: Readable says what the spices were for, as 24:1 shows.

records.source: Καὶ τὸ μὲν σάββατον ἡσύχασαν κατὰ τὴν ἐντολήν,
records.gloss: And the indeed Sabbath they rested according to the commandment,
pieces: On the Sabbath they rested, as the commandment required.

L.56: And on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

R.56: On the Sabbath day they rested, as God's law said they must.

decisions.choice: the commandment: the law of the Sabbath
decisions.reason: The law commanded rest on the seventh day (Exodus 20:8-10; Deuteronomy 5:12-14). The women kept it before going to the tomb.

decisions.choice: the sentence runs on into 24:1
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends this verse with a comma: "on the Sabbath they rested ... but on the first day of the week" (24:1). Every level ends the sentence here, because a new chapter begins.

decisions.choice: God's law said they must
decisions.reason: Readable says whose commandment it was.
